nameStory: The Big-tooth Whitelip gets its name from the distinctive white rim around its shell opening and the prominent tooth-like projections inside the aperture. These 'teeth' are actually calcium carbonate barriers that help protect the soft snail body from predators trying to reach inside the shell.
description: The Big-tooth Whitelip is a medium-sized land snail that breathes air rather than living in water. Its brown, spiral shell typically measures about an inch across and has a flattened, disc-like shape rather than a tall cone. The most striking feature is the bright white lip around the shell opening, which contrasts beautifully with the earthy tones of the rest of the shell. Like all land snails, it carries its home on its back and can retreat completely inside when threatened.

idTips.label: White shell lip
idTips.description: Look for a bright white rim around the shell opening that feels smooth and slightly thickened - this white 'lip' is the snail's signature feature and stands out clearly against darker shell colors

idTips.label: Tooth-like barriers
idTips.description: Peer into the shell opening to spot several small, white tooth-like projections that feel hard and sharp if you gently touch them with a grass blade

idTips.label: Flattened spiral shell
idTips.description: The shell has a low, disc-like profile rather than a tall spire - when viewed from the side, it's much wider than it is tall

idTips.label: Earthy shell coloration
idTips.description: The shell surface displays mottled browns and tans that feel smooth to the touch, often with subtle banding patterns that help camouflage it among leaf litter

idTips.label: Medium size
idTips.description: The shell spans roughly the width of a quarter, making it noticeably larger than many common garden snails but smaller than apple snails

habitat: Big-tooth Whitelips prefer rich, moist deciduous forests with deep leaf litter and limestone-rich soils that provide the calcium they need for shell building. Look for them in mature hardwood forests, particularly those with maple, oak, and beech trees, where they hide under logs, rocks, and thick layers of decomposing leaves. They favor areas with good moisture retention but not waterlogged conditions.

seasonality.spring: Active snails emerge from winter hiding spots as temperatures warm, often found crawling on damp mornings after rain showers. This is an excellent time to spot them moving across trails or feeding on decomposing plant matter.
seasonality.summer: During hot, dry periods they retreat deep into leaf litter or under logs and rocks, becoming mostly inactive during the day. Look for them in the coolest, shadiest, most humid spots in the forest.
seasonality.fall: Increased activity as they feed heavily before winter, often seen on overcast days or after autumn rains. Empty shells are commonly found as animals prepare for dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Snails seal themselves into their shells with a mucus barrier and remain dormant under deep leaf litter, logs, or in soil crevices until spring warmth returns.

funFact: This snail can live for over 5 years and actually grows new 'teeth' in its shell opening throughout its life - if a tooth breaks off from wear or damage, the snail can secrete new calcium carbonate to repair or replace it, essentially giving itself dental work!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative, the Eastern Whitelip, which also has a white shell lip but lacks the prominent internal teeth. Memory trick: 'Big-tooth' literally has the bigger, more obvious teeth - if you can clearly see tooth-like projections inside the shell opening, you've found the Big-tooth Whitelip.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Big-tooth,' this refers to the shell teeth, not the snail's actual feeding structure. Like all snails, it has a rasping tongue called a radula with thousands of tiny teeth for scraping food - the shell teeth are purely defensive structures.
compareHints: The Big-tooth Whitelip differs from its relative the Eastern Whitelip primarily by having multiple prominent tooth-like barriers inside the shell opening, while the Eastern Whitelip has a much smoother interior. Both share the characteristic white lip, but the Big-tooth's shell tends to be slightly more robust and the internal teeth are immediately visible when you look into the aperture.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Eastern Whitelip differs from its close relative, the Big-tooth Whitelip, primarily in the shell opening details - while both have white lips, the Big-tooth species has small tooth-like projections inside the shell opening that you can feel with your finger.
